prize_parts.citation: For the theoretical prediction of the quantum spin Hall effect and Z2 topological insulators, and the first experimental observation of the quantum spin Hall state in HgTe quantum wells

statement.case_for: I keep B028 with Kane, Mele and Molenkamp as a single achievement. Round 1 showed that four members prefer exactly this slate and that nobody disputes the reality or reproducibility of the effect. What the prize rewards is a specific chain: the Z2 invariant and the quantum spin Hall proposal in the Kane-Mele papers, then the HgTe edge-conductance measurement that turned the proposal into an observed state, then two decades of independent confirmation. The Chair asks what the citation says that 2016 did not. The 2016 prize rewarded topological phase transitions and topological phases in model systems (Thouless, Haldane, Kosterlitz). This citation concerns symmetry-protected band topology driven by spin-orbit coupling and time-reversal symmetry in real, non-magnetic materials, with no external magnetic field, a new class of quantum matter whose edge states are observed in transport. That is a distinct step and I would write the citation to say so. On the 2D versus class question I prefer a deliberately narrow 2D citation (quantum spin Hall effect and Z2 topological insulators), because it is the part the three names can honestly carry. I would not swap Mele for Hasan. Kane and Mele wrote the founding pair of papers together, and Hasan's ARPES work on the 3D strand is a separate, also decisive step that the three-person cap forces us to leave outside this year.
statement.case_against: The credit gap is real and I do not think we can fully close it. Bernevig, Hughes and Zhang made the HgTe prediction that Molenkamp's group actually tested, and the 3D strand (Fu, Kane, Mele; Moore and Balents; Roy; Hasan) is arguably the more consequential half in the community. A skeptic can also say the experimental half is thin, since the measured edge conductance was below the ideal quantised value, and that practical applications remain modest. There is a genuine risk that the committee looks like it is extending the 2016 topology prize one more time. If the committee believes the 3D strand and the Bernevig-Hughes-Zhang claim cannot be left out, then B028 may not be the right year, and I would rather move to B046 than build a four-name prize.

responses.point: Mehlig says a slate with Hasan would be at least as defensible as Kane, Mele and Molenkamp, and asks whether my doubts about circuit QED (B035) should be balanced against the Girvin and Huang omission compared with the gaps in B028.
responses.response: On Hasan, I accept that the 3D strand is large and that a sceptic can call the 2D trio narrow. But the founding theory is a Kane-Mele pair, and removing either of them to seat Hasan damages the logic of the prize more than it repairs the credit. A Kane, Molenkamp, Hasan slate, which is Ulf's version, drops the Z2 invariant's co-author. I keep the trio and make the citation explicit that it is for the quantum spin Hall effect and Z2 topological insulators, so the boundary is stated and not hidden. On your question about B035: the gap in the circuit QED credit (Girvin, Huang) is no smaller than the BHZ gap here, and I agree with you that the two are comparable in kind. I would not use that as an argument for either. I am keeping B035 out of my configuration on the overlap with 2025 and because I am recused from it, and I take B028 as the place where the committee can act now.

responses.point: Olsson prefers B046 alone with Jarillo-Herrero, MacDonald and Bistritzer, says she would not wait for the pairing mechanism, and asks whether the circuit QED step is independent enough from the 2025 tunnelling prize to stand without it.
responses.response: Thank you for the direct question. Circuit QED is a distinct step, strong coupling of a single artificial atom to a single microwave photon, but I concede the committee would have to argue that against a prize given one year ago, and I will not make that argument at the final ballot because of my recusal. On your own candidate, I agree with you that the prize is for the discovery and not for the pairing mechanism, and your swap of Andrei for Bistritzer is the cleaner credit. That moves me closer to B046 than I was in round 1. Where I still differ is maturity. Eight years is short, the superconductivity is not yet understood, and the Lopes dos Santos, Peres, Castro Neto continuum model and Andrei's STM work remain unresolved attribution claims. By comparison B028 has had twenty years of independent reproduction. I keep B046 as my first alternative and I would support it as a very close second to B028, particularly in the form you propose.

responses.point: Kroll prefers optical lattice clocks (B034, Katori and Ye) and, in the Chair's synthesis, asks himself what the discovery is beyond a capability.
responses.response: I put the same question to you in round 1 and the Chair's synthesis shows that neither you nor Eva Lindroth has yet named a finding the clocks produced that we could not have guessed. The millimetre-scale gravitational redshift and the bounds on varying constants are measurements at the new precision, not surprises from nature, and a redefinition of the second is still ahead of us. That is why I keep B034 as an alternative and not as my preference. I do agree with you on two points: the credit is the most compact on the shortlist (Katori and Ye) and reproduction across several laboratories is not in doubt. If you can cite a result at the 10^-18 level that changed a physical conclusion and not only an uncertainty budget, I would reconsider.

responses.point: Danielsson prefers two parts, Halzen alone for IceCube (B005) and MacDonald with Jarillo-Herrero for twisted bilayer graphene (B046), and asks what B028 adds beyond 2016.
responses.response: I take your 2016 question seriously and I answered it above: band topology from spin-orbit coupling in real materials without a magnetic field, with an observed edge state, is a different result from topological phases in model systems. On a two-part prize, I understand your logic about two distinct discoveries and the three-person ceiling, but the ceiling forces you to take B046 down to two names, dropping Bistritzer and Andrei, and to credit IceCube to a single person, which as you concede leaves AMANDA, DUMAND, Baikal and the collaboration outside. That trades two credit problems for one. I defer to you and Mark Pearce on the detector physics, and I still see B005 as a serious case. I would prefer a single, cleaner part with three names where I can describe the credit boundary precisely.

uncertainties: Whether the narrow 2D citation with Kane, Mele and Molenkamp will be read as an honest statement of the credit or as leaving out the more consequential 3D strand and Bernevig, Hughes and Zhang.
Whether the committee judges twisted bilayer graphene sufficiently mature despite the unsettled pairing mechanism; I have moved slightly closer to B046 but defer to the condensed-matter members.

How much weight the 2016 prize should carry against B028; I judge the achievements distinct but I am a theorist from outside condensed-matter topology and defer to Eriksson and Mehlig on the finer points.
statement.conflict_note: I direct the Wallenberg Centre for Quantum Technology, work closely with superconducting-circuit groups at Chalmers, and Chalmers hosted 2025 laureates Martinis and Clarke as guest researchers. I will recuse myself from any decision on B035. Olsson is my colleague in the Gothenburg environment, which I do not regard as a conflict for B046. I have no personal or institutional connection to B028, B046, B034, B005 or B011 beyond general scientific acquaintance, and no connection to any person credited on them.
